newsitem.title: UK: Queen unveils Wallenberg monument to rescued Jews.
newsitem.headline: Queen unveils Wallenberg monument to rescued Jews.

text.p: Queen Elizabeth, watched by Israeli President Ezer Weizman, on Wednesday unveiled a monument to Raoul Wallenberg, the Swedish diplomat who saved thousands of Jews from Nazi concentration camps in World War Two.

The ceremony to honour "the epitome of good over evil" was also attended by U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan, whose wife is a niece of Wallenberg, as well as five people who survived the Holocaust thanks to Wallenberg's bravery.
Sigmund Sternberg, the chairman of the Wallenberg Appeal Committee, described the unveiling as "a unique day of tribute to a hero of our times".
The sculpture, which follows Wallenberg memorials in Hungary, Sweden and the United States, was erected near Marble Arch in central London, close to a Jewish synagogue and the Swedish Embassy.

Created by British sculptor Philip Jackson, the monument places Wallenberg's larger-than-life figure against an enormous wall made up of thousands of Schutzpasses' -- the Swedish documents he issued to Jews to protect them from deportation.

In the last months of the war Wallenberg, who was based in Budapest as part of the Swedish legation, prevented the Nazis from taking thousands of Jews to Auschwitz by handing out passes and establishing "safe houses" flying the Swedish flag.
Inset panels on the monument describe the horrors of the Nazi regime, and inscriptions express the selflessness and courage of a man who put up to 100,000 lives before his own.
Investigations into his whereabouts have failed to discover what became of Wallenberg after he was captured by the Russians in January 1945 for his alleged links with U.S. intelligence.
Although Moscow reported Wallenberg died in prison in 1947, there have been several reports he was seen alive after that. He would be 84 if still alive.
Weizman, on the first state visit by an Israeli president to Britain, called him "the epitome of good over evil, personal courage over intimidation and selflessnes over indifference".

Following the unveiling, the presiding Rabbi of Hungary recited a memorial prayer for the Holocaust victims and five survivors rescued by Wallenberg were presented to the Queen and other heads of state.

"His selfless efforts to engineer the escape of innocent people targeted for arrest and extermination by the Nazis were undertaken at great personal risk....but he could not stand aside," Annan said of him.
"I believe that the most eloquent tribute we can pay to the memory of Raoul Wallenberg is to pursue the cause to which he devoted his life: the cause of peace, tolerance and understanding."
Also present at the unveiling was Princess Christina of Sweden, representing the King of Sweden, and the Duke of Edinburgh.
Messages from the King of Sweden and the Hungarian president paid homage to Wallenberg's services to mankind and "his stand against unspeakable oppression and tyranny".
